In this series of heritage programs, we are privileged to meet Mr. Louis Armstrong, the internationally known New Orleans jazz trumpeter and band leader. In this third program, Mr. Armstrong and his guests, Mr. Robert McCulley, writer and publicist. Mr. Adam Lynch, newscaster, TV personality and classical music broadcaster. And Mr. Benny Benack, jazz trumpeter, band leader, assistant director of the University of Pittsburgh band. We'll discuss Mr. Armstrong and the role as bandstand philosopher.
You hear so much about the Roaring Twenties, I didn't live it. Could you tell me a little bit about it?

Well, I can tell you, uh, a little, a little far back than that. I'm sure you could. Well, but this is a little far back than that. I'll say first and, uh, I guess before I joined Joe Oliver, you know, I was in New Orleans during the days, uh, of, uh, dance bands, and, uh, I noticed, uh, there were such things at the club where the members would die, you know? Yeah. And the musicians that started this up in the twenties, all from New Orleans, uh, what do you call me? Yeah. So if a member died, and, uh, they lay him out in the chapel, they get what they call a wake. You know, the body's laying out in the middle of the floor, and, and the members, and, and, and a lot of church sisters would come by, they're dressing, and you sing, and, uh, you weren't a member, you get the spirit like everybody else, because, uh, we always rejoice at the day, you know, and you probably lead off for him, see? And, uh, get everybody moving, like, late at night, you wake everybody up, you feel me? And after you get them started, you go back in the kitchen, and get you a big cup of coffee, or, a little dip, whatever there, cheese crackers, you know, and so, when the next day, when they, they, they dock him up, uh, put the top of the, the bare ribs, they got a brass band there, and, uh, after ceremonies, and, uh, the wife's crying, or the relatives, and, uh, as they bring him out the door, the brass band is, uh, you know, line up. Yeah. And then, uh, bass drum, the bass drum player, hits the drum. Boom. Sleep as a boy, and you make a step and it won. Boom. Boom. Boom. Boom. Mm-hmm . And then we'd probably go into another funeral, like, and be a prayer like that, where we get to the cemetery now. We bury this land. And after the Reverend Ash, Ash, you know, whatever they say, to cover the man up, and he pulled the snare out and rolled up, and everybody, and again, we get together, they should find their places. Oh, yeah. We're taking right to where this club, remember? And that's all of it. And then we get together. They should find their places. And then... We're this club, they're the members. And that's all it is. I suppose it's hard for a lot of us to understand, those of us who didn't see it, why the singing and why the music, but actually it was a time of rejoicing in a way. Well, Johnston, they never let a man like they would in New York, sit in the chapel, for days by themselves, there's always somebody singing. And that's why when I was way back from my time, I had the chance to remember those days. And my father used to tell me, and I'll tell you about the late, the 20s, but I was in some letters. But things was happening in Chicago before back in 1918.

segments.title: Series introduction and panel guests
segments.summary: Announcer introduces the Heritage series, Armstrong and his three guests, and tonight's topic of Armstrong as bandstand philosopher.

segments.chapter: Old New Orleans and the Twenties
segments.title: New Orleans funeral wakes, brass bands and the Roaring Twenties
segments.summary: Asked about the Twenties, Armstrong describes social club funerals, wakes and brass band processions in New Orleans, then says Chicago was jumping from 1918, before New York.

segments.chapter: Old New Orleans and the Twenties
segments.title: Health routine, mother's cooking and the hot spots today
segments.summary: Armstrong says he feels no different than before, recalls his mother's red beans and gumbo made cheaply in 1915, and says Chicago and New York have the most work for musicians.

segments.title: How youngsters can learn jazz today
segments.summary: The panel laments the lack of jam sessions; Armstrong says young players avoid older men, and recalls a boppers' remark about notes.

segments.title: The five-year-old boy backstage in Oregon
segments.summary: Armstrong tells of a small child who came to his dressing room and played the beat naturally.

segments.title: Listening to elders; Fletcher Henderson band and the Lanin and Lopez bands
segments.summary: Armstrong says he preferred the elders as a teenager, lists Fletcher Henderson band members at the Roseland at 24, and tells of hearing Sam Lanin's and Vincent Lopez's bands and an older trumpeter, B. A. Rolfe, playing seriously.

segments.title: Playing with Oliver's Chicago band and Carroll Dickerson at the Sunset
segments.summary: Armstrong credits his career to playing with good musicians, names the lineup in Chicago, the Dickerson orchestra at the Sunset, the Charleston era and the finale routine.

segments.chapter: Joe Oliver and the second line
segments.title: Joe Oliver as teacher
segments.summary: Armstrong says Oliver took time to show young musicians passages while others were too busy at the Eagle Saloon.

segments.chapter: Joe Oliver and the second line
segments.title: The second line and funeral parade customs
segments.summary: Armstrong explains the second line in parades, pool hall followers and the grand marshal, and is asked about bands meeting in the street.

segments.title: How Armstrong sees himself, audiences and records
segments.summary: Armstrong describes himself as one of the audience, discusses changing audiences and records, and why he has lasted so long.

segments.title: Feeling about music, making people happy and clowning
segments.summary: Armstrong says he is never bored with music, talks about trying to make people happy, and discusses gagging, showmanship and the note.

segments.title: Jazz abroad, working life, Crosby movies and life at home
segments.summary: Armstrong answers on jazz and diplomacy, years of touring, working schedule, the Bing Crosby film bit, his home tape collection, souvenirs and a hospital stay.
